opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most important framing questions for the whole field. If you look at the incentives, with enormous economic value, geopolitical competition, and many actors able to train frontier models, it seems very unlikely that the world coordinates to just stop. I'm not saying we shouldn't try for good governance; I think we should, and things like evaluations, compute thresholds, and responsible scaling commitments are really valuable. But as a researcher, I don't want my plan to hinge on the assumption that everyone will pause.

That pushes me toward a few things.

First, alignment research has to keep pace with capabilities. It's not enough to have a beautiful theory that's ready in thirty years if the systems we actually need to align arrive in five. So I put a lot of weight on approaches that work with the models we have now and that scale as the models get better.

Second, it makes me want to use AI to help with alignment itself. If capabilities keep improving no matter what, the question becomes whether we can turn that progress to our advantage. Can we build systems that are aligned enough, and trustworthy enough at a roughly human level, that they can do a lot of the alignment research for us? That's what the idea of an automated alignment researcher is about. The hope is that alignment progress scales with compute the same way capabilities do, rather than being bottlenecked on a small number of human researchers.

Third, it means we need to be very empirical and very honest about measurement. If you can't stop, you at least need to know where you stand. Can we actually tell whether a model is aligned? Do our techniques generalize from easy problems we can supervise to hard problems we can't? That's why I care so much about things like scalable oversight and weak-to-strong generalization, and about building evaluations that would catch us if we're wrong.

And finally, I think it puts real responsibility on the labs. If you believe development won't stop, then the people building these systems need to treat safety as a core priority, with real resources and real authority, not as an afterthought. The worst outcome would be for "it can't be stopped" to become an excuse for not taking the problem seriously. To me it means the opposite: we have to solve it, and we have to solve it in time.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most important framing questions, and I'll say upfront that my views on it have shifted over the years.

The honest starting point is that I don't think we're going to stop AI development. There's just too much economic incentive, too many actors, too many different jurisdictions. Even if you got every major lab in the US to pause tomorrow, you'd still have other countries, you'd still have open-source efforts, you'd still have the fact that the underlying compute and algorithms keep getting cheaper. So I tend to treat "development continues" as the baseline scenario, not because I think that's ideal, but because I think planning around any other assumption is a bit of wishful thinking.

And once you accept that, it really changes what alignment research should look like. The question stops being "how do we solve alignment in the abstract, with unlimited time?" and becomes "how do we make the systems that are actually going to get built as safe as possible, given the timelines we're actually on?"

A few things fall out of that for me.

The first is that you want to be working with the real systems. For a long time there was this split in the field between people doing very theoretical work on what an aligned superintelligence would look like, and people doing empirical work on the models that exist today. I used to be more sympathetic to the theoretical side, and I still think some of it matters. But if development is going to continue regardless, then the most leveraged thing you can do is be close to the frontier, understand what's actually going wrong with current models, and build techniques that scale with the capabilities as they grow. You learn a lot by trying to align a real model that you just can't learn on a whiteboard.

The second thing is that you have to be thinking about alignment as an iterative, empirical science rather than a one-shot problem. We're not going to get one chance to get it right at the end. We get many chances along the way, and each generation of models is both a test bed and a warning system. So the research agenda should be designed to extract as much signal as possible from each generation. That's part of why I've been so focused on things like scalable oversight and using models to help with alignment research itself. If you can't stop the capabilities from growing, you want the alignment effort to grow with them, and the most plausible way to do that is to have AI systems doing a lot of the alignment work.

The third thing, and this is maybe where I'd push back a little on how the question is sometimes framed, is that "we can't stop development" doesn't mean "we can't shape it." There's a lot of space between a full pause and a free-for-all. You can slow specific deployments, you can build evaluations that create natural checkpoints, you can push for norms around what capabilities you don't release until you've demonstrated certain safety properties. Alignment research that produces concrete, measurable evaluations actually gives you leverage here, because it turns a vague "this feels risky" into "this model fails this test, so we don't ship it." That's a much more defensible position, both inside a company and in a policy conversation.

And then the last thing I'd say is that it should make you humble about what counts as success. If the realistic path is continued development, then the goal isn't to have a complete theory of alignment before any powerful system exists. The goal is to make sure that at every step, we understand the systems well enough to catch the important failures, and that we have enough slack in the system that when we do catch something, we can actually act on it. Some people find that unsatisfying. I find it motivating, honestly, because it means the work you do this year actually matters for what gets deployed next year, rather than being a bet on some far-off scenario.

So in short: the difficulty of stopping development is a reason to do more empirical, more iterative, more leverage-seeking alignment research, and to stay close enough to the frontier that your work actually affects what gets built.

astra-6.text:
I think it means we should aim for alignment techniques that are practical to adopt. If your plan depends on everyone stopping AI development for a long time while we solve alignment, then you’ve made your success depend on something that seems very difficult to achieve.

So I’d want to ask: Can we develop techniques that work with the systems people are actually building? Can we make them sufficiently efficient that using them doesn’t put you at a huge disadvantage? And can we give developers good evidence about whether those techniques are working?

That doesn’t mean we should assume development must continue at any speed, regardless of the risks. There could be situations where slowing down or not deploying a system is really important. But as an alignment researcher, I think you want to make the tradeoff less painful: make it easier to build systems safely, and make it clearer when we don’t yet know how to do that.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it pushes you toward doing research that can work under the conditions you actually expect to face. If your plan depends on everyone stopping development for several years at exactly the right moment, that’s a pretty strong assumption. You’d want to ask: can we make this work with the systems people are building, with the time and resources we’re likely to have?

That makes me interested in approaches where increasingly capable AI systems help us with alignment research. Human oversight is already limited, and that problem gets harder as the systems become more capable. So we need ways to extend our ability to evaluate what they’re doing, find mistakes, and understand whether our training methods are producing the behavior we actually want.

But I wouldn’t conclude that we should just accept whatever pace of development happens. There’s a distinction between saying that a global stop would be difficult and saying that a particular lab shouldn’t slow down or stop when it sees evidence of danger. We should work on the technical problem while also making it easier to make those decisions responsibly. The difficulty of coordination is a constraint on an alignment strategy, not a reason to assume we’ll somehow solve alignment in time.
